# From Measurements to a Curve

## The Fitting Problem

We have measurements
$$
(x_i,y_i\pm \sigma_i),
\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,
$$
and a model
$$
y=f(x;\boldsymbol\theta).
$$

We need to:

::: incremental
- estimate the parameters $\boldsymbol\theta$;
- determine their uncertainties and correlations;
- check whether the model agrees with the data;
- examine the residuals and the stability of the result.
:::

## Why One Cannot Simply Draw a Nice Curve

::: incremental
- The points have different uncertainties.
- The errors of different points may be correlated.
- The model parameters also turn out to be correlated.
- An outlier or a wrong model can strongly bias the result.
- A good-looking picture does not replace a quantitative goodness-of-fit test.
:::

::: {.fragment .callout-note .thmbox appearance="simple"}
A fit is a statistical procedure, not a graphical way of drawing a line between points.
:::


# Connection with the Likelihood Method

## Gaussian Model of Measurements

Let $x_i$ be known exactly, and let the measurements $y_i$ be independent and **Gaussian distributed**:
$$
Y_i
\sim
\mathrm N\!\left(
f(x_i;\boldsymbol\theta),
\sigma_i^2
\right).
$$

Then the likelihood function is
$$
L(\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{N}
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_i}
\exp\!\left[
-\frac{
[y_i-f(x_i;\boldsymbol\theta)]^2
}{2\sigma_i^2}
\right].
$$

## Weighted Sum of Squares

For known $\sigma_i$ that do not depend on the parameters:
$$
-2\ln L(\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\frac{
[y_i-f(x_i;\boldsymbol\theta)]^2
}{\sigma_i^2}
+\mathrm{const}.
$$

Therefore maximizing the likelihood is equivalent to minimizing
$$
\boxed{
\chi^2(\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\frac{[y_i-f(x_i;\boldsymbol\theta)]^2}{\sigma_i^2}.
}
$$


## What the Weights Mean

Contribution of a single point:
$$
\chi_i^2
=\frac{[y_i-f(x_i;\boldsymbol\theta)]^2}{\sigma_i^2}\equiv
\frac{r_i^2}{\sigma_i^2}.
$$

::: incremental
- A point with small $\sigma_i$ has a stronger influence on the fit.
- A point with large $\sigma_i$ allows a larger absolute residual.
- The weight of a point equals the inverse variance:
  $$
  w_i=\frac{1}{\sigma_i^2}.
  $$
- The weight must follow from the probabilistic model, not be chosen to obtain a desired result.
:::


## Least Squares Is Not Universal

Least squares arises naturally in the Gaussian approximation. It may be wrong if:

::: incremental
- small Poisson counts are observed;
- the distribution has heavy tails;
- the errors are asymmetric;
- there are physical boundaries;
- the variance depends on the parameters, but this is ignored;
- the uncertainties along the $x$ axis are significant.
:::


# A Straight Line Through Points

## Linear Model

Consider
$$
y_i=a+b x_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i\sim\mathrm N(0,\sigma_i^2).
$$

We minimize
$$
\chi^2(a,b)
=
\sum_i w_i(y_i-a-bx_i)^2,
\qquad
w_i=\frac1{\sigma_i^2}.
$$

Conditions for the minimum:
$$
\frac{\partial\chi^2}{\partial a}=0,
\qquad
\frac{\partial\chi^2}{\partial b}=0.
$$

## Derivation of the Normal Equations

We differentiate
$$
\chi^2(a,b)=\sum_i w_i(y_i-a-bx_i)^2.
$$

We obtain two conditions:
$$
\frac{\partial\chi^2}{\partial a}
=
-2\sum_i w_i(y_i-a-bx_i)=0,
$$
$$
\frac{\partial\chi^2}{\partial b}
=
-2\sum_i w_i x_i(y_i-a-bx_i)=0.
$$

We expand the brackets and move the known quantities to the right-hand side:
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
\sum_iw_i&\sum_iw_ix_i\\
\sum_iw_ix_i&\sum_iw_ix_i^2
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sum_iw_iy_i\\
\sum_iw_ix_iy_i
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

## Normal Equations

Let us introduce the sums
$$
\begin{aligned}
S&=\sum_iw_i,
&
S_x&=\sum_iw_ix_i,
&
S_y&=\sum_iw_iy_i,\\
S_{xx}&=\sum_iw_ix_i^2,
&
S_{xy}&=\sum_iw_ix_iy_i.
\end{aligned}
$$

Then
$$
\begin{pmatrix}
S&S_x\\
S_x&S_{xx}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}S_y\\S_{xy}\end{pmatrix}.
$$

## Formal Solution

Let us write the system more compactly:
$$
A\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf c,
\qquad
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
S&S_x\\
S_x&S_{xx}
\end{pmatrix},
\quad
\boldsymbol\beta=
\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\end{pmatrix},
\quad
\mathbf c=
\begin{pmatrix}S_y\\S_{xy}\end{pmatrix}.
$$

If the matrix $A$ is invertible, then
$$
\boxed{
\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=
A^{-1}\mathbf c.
}
$$

::: {.fragment .callout-note .thmbox appearance="simple"}
Invertibility means that the data really distinguish $a$ and $b$.
For example, if all points have the same $x$, the slope cannot be determined.
:::

## Covariance of the Parameters

From the lecture [on the two-dimensional Gaussian](lecture-07-two-dimensional-gaussian.qmd) we know the form of the multivariate Gaussian:
$$
p(\boldsymbol\beta)
\propto
\exp\!\left[
-\frac12
(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})^\mathsf T
V_\beta^{-1}
(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
\right].
$$

And for Gaussian measurement errors
$$
L(\boldsymbol\beta)
\propto
\exp\!\left[-\frac12\chi^2(\boldsymbol\beta)\right].
$$

So near the minimum we need to recognize in $\chi^2$ the quadratic form
$$
\boxed{
\chi^2(\boldsymbol\beta)
\approx
\chi^2_{\min}
+
(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})^\mathsf T
V_\beta^{-1}
(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}).
}
$$

## Covariance of the Parameters for a Straight Line

For a straight line, $\chi^2$ is a quadratic function of the parameters, so this is not an approximation but an exact equality:
$$
\chi^2(\boldsymbol\beta)
=
\chi^2_{\min}
+
(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})^\mathsf T
\begin{pmatrix}
S&S_x\\
S_x&S_{xx}
\end{pmatrix}
(\boldsymbol\beta-\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}).
$$

Comparing with the form of the multivariate Gaussian, we obtain
$$
\boxed{
V_\beta^{-1}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
S&S_x\\
S_x&S_{xx}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
V_\beta
=
\begin{pmatrix}
S&S_x\\
S_x&S_{xx}
\end{pmatrix}^{-1}.
}
$$

## Explicit Formulas for the Estimates

Let us denote
$$
\Delta=SS_{xx}-S_x^2.
$$

Then from $\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=V_\beta\mathbf c$ we obtain
$$
\boxed{
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat a\\
\widehat b
\end{pmatrix}
=
V_\beta
\begin{pmatrix}
S_y\\S_{xy}
\end{pmatrix}
=
\frac1\Delta
\begin{pmatrix}
S_{xx}S_y-S_xS_{xy}\\
SS_{xy}-S_xS_y
\end{pmatrix}.
}
$$

## Explicit Formulas for the Covariances

Recall:
$$
S=\sum_iw_i,\qquad
S_x=\sum_iw_ix_i,\qquad
S_{xx}=\sum_iw_ix_i^2,
\qquad
\Delta=SS_{xx}-S_x^2.
$$

The matrix $V_\beta$ is the covariance matrix of the parameter vector:
$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat a\\
\widehat b
\end{pmatrix}
\right)
=
V_\beta.
}
$$

Explicitly
$$
\boxed{
V_\beta
=
\frac1\Delta
\begin{pmatrix}
S_{xx}&-S_x\\
-S_x&S
\end{pmatrix}.
}
$$

Its elements:
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat a)=\frac{S_{xx}}{\Delta},
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat b)=\frac{S}{\Delta},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat a,\widehat b)=-\frac{S_x}{\Delta}.
$$

## What the Errors Depend On

Let us introduce the weighted center and the weighted spread in $x$:
$$
\bar x_w=\frac{S_x}{S},
\qquad
Q_x=\sum_iw_i(x_i-\bar x_w)^2=\frac{\Delta}{S}.
$$

Then the same formulas can be rewritten as:
$$
\boxed{
\sigma_b^2=\frac{1}{Q_x},
\qquad
\sigma_a^2=\frac{1}{S}+\frac{\bar x_w^2}{Q_x},
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat a,\widehat b)=-\frac{\bar x_w}{Q_x}.
}
$$

::: incremental
- Smaller errors of the points give larger weights $w_i=1/\sigma_i^2$ and reduce the errors of the parameters.
- The slope is determined by the lever arm $Q_x$: the more widely the points are spread in $x$, the smaller $\sigma_b$.
- The intercept $a$ refers to the point $x=0$. If the data are far from zero, the error of the slope propagates into the error of $a$.
- The covariance appears because a change in the slope is compensated by a shift of the intercept.
:::

## Center of Gravity of the Points
::: incremental
- At fixed slope $b$, minimizing $\chi^2$ with respect to $a$:
$$
0=\frac{\partial\chi^2}{\partial a}
=
-2\sum_iw_i(y_i-a-bx_i).
$$

- Hence
$$
\boxed{
a(b)=\bar y_w-b\bar x_w,
\qquad
\bar y_w=\frac{\sum_iw_iy_i}{\sum_iw_i}.
}
$$

- The best line for any $b$ passes through the "center of gravity"
$$
(\bar x_w,\bar y_w).
$$

- The next step is to find the $b$ that minimizes $\chi^2$.
:::

## Error geometry: profiling over $a$ {#applet-fit-geometry}

::: {.clt-widget}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false

viewof geomXbar = Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 1.8, step: 0.1, label: "center x̄_w"})
viewof geomSpread = Inputs.range([0.45, 2.5], {value: 1.0, step: 0.05, label: "spread in x"})

geomS = 18
geomQx = geomS * geomSpread * geomSpread
geomSigmaB = 1 / Math.sqrt(geomQx)
geomSigmaA = Math.sqrt(1 / geomS + geomXbar * geomXbar / geomQx)
geomCovAB = -geomXbar / geomQx
geomCorrAB = geomCovAB / (geomSigmaA * geomSigmaB)

geomA0 = 1.0
geomB0 = 0.55
geomYbar = geomA0 + geomB0 * geomXbar
geomSlopeSteps = [-1, 0, 1]
geomLineData = geomSlopeSteps.flatMap(k => {
  const b = geomB0 + k * geomSigmaB;
  const a = geomYbar - b * geomXbar;
  return Array.from({length: 121}, (_, i) => {
    const x = -4.5 + 9 * i / 120;
    return {x, y: a + b * x, k};
  });
})
geomFanLineData = geomLineData.filter(d => d.k !== 0)
geomBestLineData = geomLineData.filter(d => d.k === 0)

geomOffsets = [-1.55, -1.05, -0.55, -0.12, 0.35, 0.82, 1.28, 1.62]
geomPointSigma = Math.sqrt(geomOffsets.length / geomS)
geomResidualPattern = [0.09, -0.04, 0.06, -0.08, 0.02, 0.07, -0.05, -0.07]
geomPoints = geomOffsets.map((u, i) => {
  const x = geomXbar + geomSpread * u;
  return {x, y: geomA0 + geomB0 * x + geomResidualPattern[i]};
})

geomCenterPoint = [{x: geomXbar, y: geomYbar}]
geomLabels = [
  {x: 0, y: 3.25, text: "x = 0"},
  {x: geomXbar, y: 3.0, text: "data center"}
]

geomDataPlot = Plot.plot({
  width: 650,
  height: 420,
  marginLeft: 58,
  marginBottom: 46,
  x: {label: "x", domain: [-4.5, 4.5], grid: true},
  y: {label: "y", domain: [-2.0, 3.5], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "#aaa", strokeDasharray: "6,5"}),
    Plot.ruleX([geomXbar], {stroke: "#ffb347", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.line(geomFanLineData, {x: "x", y: "y", z: "k", stroke: "#70b7ff", strokeWidth: 2.4, strokeOpacity: 0.58}),
    Plot.line(geomBestLineData, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#ffb347", strokeWidth: 4}),
    Plot.ruleX(geomPoints, {x: "x", y1: d => d.y - geomPointSigma, y2: d => d.y + geomPointSigma, stroke: "#aaa", strokeOpacity: 0.65}),
    Plot.dot(geomPoints, {x: "x", y: "y", r: 6, fill: "#4ea1ff", fillOpacity: 0.82}),
    Plot.dot(geomCenterPoint, {x: "x", y: "y", r: 8, fill: "#ffb347", stroke: "#111", strokeWidth: 1}),
    Plot.text(geomLabels, {x: "x", y: "y", text: "text", fill: "#f2f2f2", fontSize: 16, dy: -8})
  ]
})

geomSa2 = geomSigmaA * geomSigmaA
geomSb2 = geomSigmaB * geomSigmaB
geomL11 = geomSigmaA
geomL21 = geomCovAB / geomL11
geomL22 = Math.sqrt(Math.max(geomSb2 - geomL21 * geomL21, 0))
geomLevel = Math.sqrt(2.30)
geomEllipse = Array.from({length: 241}, (_, i) => {
  const t = 2 * Math.PI * i / 240;
  const z1 = geomLevel * Math.cos(t);
  const z2 = geomLevel * Math.sin(t);
  return {
    da: geomL11 * z1,
    db: geomL21 * z1 + geomL22 * z2
  };
})
geomDaMax = Math.max(0.55, 1.18 * Math.max(...geomEllipse.map(d => Math.abs(d.da))))
geomDbMax = Math.max(0.42, 1.18 * Math.max(...geomEllipse.map(d => Math.abs(d.db))))
geomCompLine = [
  {db: -geomDbMax, da: geomXbar * geomDbMax},
  {db: geomDbMax, da: -geomXbar * geomDbMax}
]

geomParamPlot = Plot.plot({
  width: 560,
  height: 420,
  marginLeft: 66,
  marginBottom: 46,
  x: {label: "δa", domain: [-geomDaMax, geomDaMax], grid: true},
  y: {label: "δb", domain: [-geomDbMax, geomDbMax], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "#888"}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#888"}),
    Plot.line(geomEllipse, {x: "da", y: "db", stroke: "#ffb347", strokeWidth: 4}),
    Plot.line(geomCompLine, {x: "da", y: "db", stroke: "#70b7ff", strokeWidth: 3, strokeDasharray: "7,5"}),
    Plot.dot([{da: 0, db: 0}], {x: "da", y: "db", r: 6, fill: "#f2f2f2"})
  ]
})

html`
<div class="clt-panel">
  <div style="display:flex; gap:0.9rem; align-items:center; justify-content:center;">
    ${geomDataPlot}
    ${geomParamPlot}
  </div>
  <div class="clt-summary">
    <span>Q_x = ${geomQx.toFixed(1)}</span>
    <span>σ_y fixed: ${geomPointSigma.toFixed(2)}</span>
    <span>σ_b = ${geomSigmaB.toFixed(3)}</span>
    <span>σ_a = ${geomSigmaA.toFixed(3)}</span>
    <span>corr(a,b) = ${geomCorrAB.toFixed(2)}</span>
  </div>
</div>
`
```
:::

::: {.fragment .callout-note .thmbox appearance="simple"}
The blue lines are the best lines at slopes $\widehat b\pm\sigma_b$: for each slope the intercept $a$ re-minimizes $\chi^2$. Therefore they pass through the center of the data but describe the points worse than the orange line.
:::

## Centered parametrization

The correlation is visible directly from the formula
$$
\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat a,\widehat b)=-\frac{\bar x_w}{Q_x}.
$$

If we move the origin to the weighted center of the data,
$$
x_i'=x_i-\bar x_w,
\qquad
\bar x_w=\frac{\sum_iw_ix_i}{\sum_iw_i},
$$
and write the same line as
$$
y=a'+b'x',
\qquad
a'=a+b\bar x_w,
\qquad
b'=b,
$$
then for the new parameters
$$
S_x'=\sum_iw_ix_i'=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat a',\widehat b')=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat a')=\frac1S,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\widehat b')=\frac1{Q_x}.
$$

::: {.fragment .callout-note .thmbox appearance="simple"}
$a'$ is the value of the line at the center of the data, not the old intercept at $x=0$.
The parametrization affects the correlation but does not change the physical line.
:::

## Connection to normal coordinates

In centered parameters the quadratic form near the minimum is diagonal:
$$
\Delta\chi^2
=
\chi^2(a',b')-\chi^2_{\min}
=
S\,(\delta a')^2
+
Q_x\,(\delta b')^2.
$$

There is no cross term $\delta a'\delta b'$, which means the parameters are uncorrelated.

If we also go over to dimensionless coordinates
$$
z_a=\sqrt{S}\,\delta a'
=
\frac{\delta a'}{\sigma_{a'}},
\qquad
z_b=\sqrt{Q_x}\,\delta b'
=
\frac{\delta b'}{\sigma_{b'}},
$$
then
$$
\boxed{
\Delta\chi^2=z_a^2+z_b^2.
}
$$

::: {.fragment .callout-note .thmbox appearance="simple"}
These are precisely the normal coordinates for the local Gaussian of the parameters: first we diagonalize the form, then we measure the axes in units of their standard errors.
:::

## An outlier spoils the fit. Interactive

The applet generates points around the line
$$
y=1+0.8x
$$
and performs a weighted fit.

::: incremental
1. We change the statistical error of the points.
2. We add a controllable outlier.
3. We compare the fitted line with the true one.
4. We look at the residuals and the contribution of the outlier to $\chi^2$.
:::

## Interactive: line, errors and outlier {#applet-line-outlier}

::: {.clt-widget}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false

viewof lsSigma = Inputs.range([0.15, 1.5], {value: 0.55, step: 0.05, label: "typical error sigma"})
viewof lsOutlier = Inputs.range([-4, 6], {value: 0, step: 0.25, label: "shift of one point"})
viewof regenerateLs = Inputs.button("New data")

randnLs = () => {
  const u1 = Math.max(Math.random(), 1e-12);
  const u2 = Math.random();
  return Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(u1)) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * u2);
}

lsData = {
  regenerateLs;
  const data = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 16; ++i) {
    const x = -4.5 + 9 * i / 15;
    const sigma = lsSigma * (0.72 + 0.56 * (i % 4) / 3);
    const y = 1 + 0.8 * x + sigma * randnLs() + (i === 12 ? lsOutlier : 0);
    data.push({x, y, sigma, outlier: i === 12});
  }
  return data;
}

weightedLineFit = data => {
  let S = 0, Sx = 0, Sy = 0, Sxx = 0, Sxy = 0;
  for (const d of data) {
    const w = 1 / (d.sigma * d.sigma);
    S += w;
    Sx += w * d.x;
    Sy += w * d.y;
    Sxx += w * d.x * d.x;
    Sxy += w * d.x * d.y;
  }
  const delta = S * Sxx - Sx * Sx;
  const a = (Sxx * Sy - Sx * Sxy) / delta;
  const b = (S * Sxy - Sx * Sy) / delta;
  const chi2 = data.reduce((sum, d) => sum + ((d.y - a - b * d.x) / d.sigma) ** 2, 0);
  return {a, b, chi2, sigmaA: Math.sqrt(Sxx / delta), sigmaB: Math.sqrt(S / delta), covAB: -Sx / delta};
}

lsFit = weightedLineFit(lsData)
lsFitLine = Array.from({length: 201}, (_, i) => {
  const x = -5 + 10 * i / 200;
  return {x, y: lsFit.a + lsFit.b * x};
})
lsTrueLine = Array.from({length: 201}, (_, i) => {
  const x = -5 + 10 * i / 200;
  return {x, y: 1 + 0.8 * x};
})
lsResiduals = lsData.map(d => ({
  x: d.x,
  pull: (d.y - lsFit.a - lsFit.b * d.x) / d.sigma,
  outlier: d.outlier
}))

lsMainPlot = Plot.plot({
  width: 720,
  height: 460,
  marginLeft: 65,
  x: {label: "x", domain: [-5, 5], grid: true},
  y: {label: "y", grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(lsData, {x: "x", y1: d => d.y - d.sigma, y2: d => d.y + d.sigma, stroke: "#aaa"}),
    Plot.dot(lsData, {x: "x", y: "y", r: 6, fill: d => d.outlier ? "#ff6b6b" : "#4ea1ff"}),
    Plot.line(lsTrueLine, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#999", strokeDasharray: "7,5", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.line(lsFitLine, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "#ffb347", strokeWidth: 4})
  ]
})

lsResidualPlot = Plot.plot({
  width: 520,
  height: 460,
  marginLeft: 65,
  x: {label: "x", domain: [-5, 5], grid: true},
  y: {label: "residual / sigma", domain: [-6, 6], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "#f2f2f2"}),
    Plot.ruleY([-2, 2], {stroke: "#999", strokeDasharray: "6,5"}),
    Plot.dot(lsResiduals, {x: "x", y: "pull", r: 6, fill: d => d.outlier ? "#ff6b6b" : "#4ea1ff"})
  ]
})

html`
<div class="clt-panel">
  <div style="display:flex; gap:0.7rem; justify-content:center; align-items:center;">
    ${lsMainPlot}
    ${lsResidualPlot}
  </div>
  <div class="clt-summary">
    <span>a_hat = ${lsFit.a.toFixed(3)} ± ${lsFit.sigmaA.toFixed(3)}</span>
    <span>b_hat = ${lsFit.b.toFixed(3)} ± ${lsFit.sigmaB.toFixed(3)}</span>
    <span>χ²_min = ${lsFit.chi2.toFixed(1)}</span>
  </div>
</div>
`
```
:::

## What the applet shows

::: incremental
- Without an outlier the fitted line fluctuates around the true one.
- Increasing the errors weakens the constraints on the parameters.
- A single distant outlier noticeably shifts the line and increases $\chi^2$.
- The residuals reveal structure that is easy to miss on the main plot.
- Ordinary least squares is not a method that is robust to outliers.
:::

# What is important to remember

## Summary

::: incremental
- Least squares arises from a Gaussian likelihood.
- In a linear model the parameter estimates are found from the normal equations.
- The covariance of the parameters is determined by the geometry of the points and the measurement errors.
- Residuals are essential for diagnosing the fit.
:::
